source.title: Exploring the Limits of Large Scale Pre-training
source.authors: Samira Abnar; Mostafa Dehghani; Behnam Neyshabur; Hanie Sedghi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. Many plotted results are supplied only as figure descriptions, without readable underlying values.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different modality and different measures from language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling: supervised image-task accuracy and downstream transfer performance. It directly tests whether downstream performance is predictable from upstream performance or scaling, and whether fitted relationships vary by setup.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure language-model cross-entropy loss or the parameter/token/compute loss laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim. It reports its own image-task results on downstream accuracy, fitted downstream-versus-upstream error curves, and controlled scale sweeps. Cited language-model scaling results are not treated as findings from this study.
record.test_reason: In image models (ViT, Mixer, ResNet; 10M–10B parameters) the study measures how downstream few-shot and fine-tuning accuracy tracks upstream accuracy and controlled scale. It argues explicitly that downstream gains saturate and can run opposite to upstream gains, so V6 needs restating. This is a new modality and a different measure (accuracy, not loss), so it bears on V6 only. It fits no pretraining-loss law in parameters, tokens or compute (V1–V5), and its fitting-choice results concern its own downstream-vs-upstream law, not published loss-law exponents (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that as upstream accuracy improves, whether by scaling or by hyperparameter and architecture choices, downstream performance saturates, often well below 100%. Scaling affects downstream mainly through upstream accuracy. Some head hyperparameters put upstream and downstream at odds. No single checkpoint suits all tasks, and data diversity should be treated as an additional axis of scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes supervised image-model accuracy and few-shot/fine-tuning transfer, fitting downstream error against upstream error. It does not fit language-model held-out cross-entropy against parameters, tokens, or compute, or find a compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that fitted parameters vary with upstream and downstream task and shot count; fit prediction error differs between convex-hull fitting and fitting all data; downstream outcomes also vary with head weight decay, head learning rate, and shot count.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameters of the downstream-vs-upstream power law (k, alpha, eIR) vary with upstream task, downstream task and shot count; eIR falls as shots increase (Table 2, Figures 3, 15, 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The parameters of downstream-vs-upstream transfer laws depend on the task pair and the amount of downstream data.

record.problems: The main evidence is a meta-study of models originally trained for other purposes, not a systematic grid search designed for this analysis. The authors note potential hyperparameter-selection biases. Many key outcomes are shown in plots without exact values in the supplied text, and the work concerns supervised image recognition rather than language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every downstream dataset, model configuration, head-weight-decay value, or head-learning-rate value. The paper reports many such results in Figures 27, 32, 34–42, but the supplied text gives mostly aggregate descriptions or figure-only plots; representative aggregate findings and explicitly stated condition effects are retained.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute is fitted.
No extrapolation of loss to much larger runs.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison of loss.
Upstream image accuracy or loss is never fitted as a power law in scale; only downstream-vs-upstream accuracy is fitted.
No fitting or setup dependence of pretraining-loss exponents or the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Per-task root squared error of downstream accuracy predicted from upstream accuracy via Eq. 1 in the controlled experiments. Values range from 0.049 (smallnorb) to 0.446 (retinopathy); kitti 0.438, camelyon 0.402. Predictability is poor on some tasks.

VTAB-1K fine-tuning of ViT-B/32 with head weight decay 0 vs 5: cifar100 0.51→0.79, sun397 0.42→0.65, clevr-count 0.72→0.42, VTAB-ALL 0.69→0.68. Downstream effects of a pretraining choice differ in sign across tasks.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-linked rows to V7. The paper's fitting-choice and parameter-variation results concern its own downstream-vs-upstream accuracy law, not pretraining-loss exponents, so V7 is untested. Tranche changed to T5 because the paper explicitly argues against unbounded, predictable downstream transfer. The main evidence is a meta-study of models trained for other purposes, with possible hyperparameter-selection bias.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute loss scaling, or loss-law bottleneck conditions are measured.
The study predicts downstream image accuracy from upstream image accuracy, not held-out loss of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal trend is measured.
The study does not compare held-out loss at fixed parameter count while isolating depth, width, or other architecture details.
Although the paper studies supervised image pretraining and transfer, it does not measure whether the held-out pretraining-loss scaling law from language models holds in other modalities or regimes.
The study tests image downstream accuracy against image upstream accuracy and scale, not downstream performance against language-model pretraining loss.

The study tests setup and fitting dependence for its image downstream-versus-upstream accuracy relationship. It does not test parameter-counting choices, language-model training schedules or loss-law fits, disagreement between the original language-model laws, or compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: ViT-B/32
rows.operation_detail: Varied upstream-head weight decay while keeping weight decay for the rest of the network at 0.01.

conditions.value: 1, 5, 10, and 20 in the study's few-shot settings
multiple image tasks; 25 tasks in the appendix

rows.value: The text reports that head-weight-decay optima differ between upstream and downstream tasks and among downstream tasks; beyond the upstream optimum, increasing decay can worsen upstream accuracy while improving some downstream tasks. The effect is stronger at lower shot counts.
rows.note: The reported outcomes vary by downstream task and shot count; figures do not provide readable exact values in the supplied text.
rows.check: For some downstream tasks, raising head weight decay lowers upstream accuracy while raising downstream accuracy. That is opposite to downstream tracking pretraining performance. It is task-dependent, not universal. Remap from V7 to V6.
